title: Chebyshev Type II Filter (CHEBY2)
summary: A second order recursive lowpass with zeros placed among fast swings, rescaled so a flat price passes unchanged; the attenuation setting shapes how it treats the fastest noise.
description:
The Chebyshev Type II Filter is a recursive second order lowpass built from a Type II analogue design: two poles that set the smoothing and a pair of zeros that remove one band of fast swings almost completely.

The cutoff is wc = 2 pi / length, pre-warped to 2 tan(wc / 2). The *Stopband Attenuation* in decibels sets epsilon = 1 / sqrt(10 ^ (attenuation / 10) - 1), which places the poles, and the zeros sit at sqrt(2) times the pre-warped cutoff. The design is mapped to a digital biquad with the bilinear transform, and the numerator is then rescaled so the filter has a gain of exactly one for a flat price. Each bar's output combines the current and two previous prices with the two previous outputs. The first two bars are seeded with the price, and a missing price counts as zero.

As computed here, the filter passes swings longer than about 0.8 times the length almost unchanged, halves the power of swings near 0.6 times the length, and wipes out swings near 0.4 times the length (about 4 bars at the default length of 10). The very fastest swings, two bars long, come through at 10 ^ (attenuation / 20) / 4 times their size: about 0.45 at the default 5 dB, one at about 12 dB, and larger than one above that.
howToRead:
At the default settings, use it as a smooth line that tracks the price level closely. Price above a rising line shows an upward short-term direction and below a falling line a downward one; turns in the line mark changes in the smoothed direction. A longer length smooths more and turns later.

Treat the attenuation setting with care, because it does not behave like a simple strength dial. Raising it above about 12 dB makes the line amplify the fastest bar to bar zigzags, so it becomes noisier than price itself (at 20 dB it is already rougher than the close, and at very high values it swings wildly). Lowering it below about 3 dB adds a bump that enlarges swings a little shorter than the length, by up to about 68 percent at 1 dB. Values around the default of 5 dB keep the line both smooth and flat.

settings.label: Length
settings.description: The cutoff period in bars. Every feature of the response scales with it: a longer length smooths more and reacts later.

settings.label: Stopband Attenuation (dB)
settings.description: Places the poles of the design. Around 5 dB the line is smooth and flat; well above 12 dB the fastest two-bar swings are amplified, and below about 3 dB swings near the cutoff are enlarged.

settings.label: Source
settings.description: The price series the filter smooths. The close by default.

faq.q: Why does a high attenuation make the line noisier?
faq.a: After the numerator is rescaled for a flat price, the gain for the fastest two-bar swings works out to 10 ^ (attenuation / 20) / 4. That is below one only up to about 12 dB; above it those swings are enlarged rather than removed.

faq.q: How does it differ from the Type I filter?
faq.a: Type I has a bump at the cutoff and puts both its zeros at the fastest two-bar swing, so its cut keeps deepening toward the fastest swings. This filter places its zeros at a band of fast swings near 0.4 times the length and removes that band almost completely, and at moderate attenuation its response for slower swings stays nearly flat.
After the transform the filter's gain for a flat price is not exactly one. Rescaling makes a flat price come out unchanged, so the line sits on the price level rather than above or below it.
